an3.61:1.1: This is the only occurrence of the phrase “sectarian tenet” (_titthāyatana_). | _Tittha_, literally “ford”, is a path to salvation, used as a term for a non-Buddhist “religion”. _Titthakara_ is a “religious founder” (literally “ford-maker”); _titthiya_ is a “monastic of (another) religion” (for example at [pli-tv-bu-vb-np22:1.2.5]()); _titthiyasāvaka_ is a “disciple of a monastic of (another) religion”. | _Āyatana_ here is literally “home ground”, the defining belief or “tenet” of a religious community. | In the phrase _parampi gantvā_, the commentary glosses _parampi_ as “lineage” (_paramparā_), with the explanation, “Even if they have gone to one of the three kinds of lineage, the lineage of teachers, the lineage of beliefs, and the lineage of reincarnation.” The latter presumably means that one follows the same path as in a past life. Bodhi (*Numerical Discourses*) rejects this, takes _parampi_ as “further” and translates “taken to their conclusion”. Elsewhere, however, the expression _parampi gantvā_ is used of a slave who belongs to their original master “even having gone to another” ([ja546:103.4]()). While I agree with Bodhi that the commentarial gloss is dubious if taken literally, I think it’s on the right track. The point is that even if one converts to another religion it will end up a waste of time.
an3.61:1.4: This view was held by Jains. The view that all experiences are caused by past kamma is consistently rejected in the Suttas (eg. [an3.61:2.1](), [mn101:2.5](). This is reflected in the later Theravada commentaries, which describe five interacting _niyāmas_, or systems of natural law: seasons (_utu_), genetics (_bīja_), moral or immoral deeds (_kamma_), mind (_citta_), and principles of the teaching (_dhamma_). Nonetheless, the view that all experiences are caused by kamma is common among modern Buddhists, and is often heard even from learned scholars. This is a harmful misunderstanding, as it has led to discrimination against the poor and disabled in Buddhist countries. One point of confusion is that rebirth into a particular life is caused by kamma, so in that general sense, kamma is a necessary condition for having a life in which one can experience anything. But the feelings experienced in that life are caused by a variety of things, not necessarily by kamma. | Note the use of _purisapuggala_ (“individual person”) as a Jain idiom. See [mn35:10.7]() and note, and [sn22.22]() and notes.
an3.61:1.6: Also at [mn101:22.5](). | _Issara_ (“God Almighty”) is the personal deity who created the world ([dn24:2.14.1]()), characterized by his “lordship” and “sovereignty” rather than, as with _brahmā_, his immanent divinity. He rarely appears in pre-Buddhist texts, where the creator is usually said to be Brahmā or Pajāpatī. _Issara_ was sometimes a polytheistic conception, appearing in plural as a generic term for heavenly “sovereigns” (Atharva Veda 7.102, 12.3.42), while the monotheistic sense “sovereign overlord” also appears in the same text (11.4.1, 11.4.10, 19.6.4, 19.53.8). This became one of the terms exalting the unborn Self as “lord of all” (_sarveśvara_, Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). The current Sutta refutes the key tenet of the monotheist Śvetāśvatara, who lived within a few centuries of the Buddha. He used Īśvara in the sense “Supreme Lord” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7), who was the creator of all (6.16), including pleasure and pain (1.2).
an3.61:1.8: This was a view of the Ājīvikas, led by bamboo-staffed ascetic Gosāla, leader of the Ājīvikas ([dn2:20.3]()), and also Pūraṇa Kassapa ([sn22.60:2.2]()). Instead beings experience pleasure and pain because they are “molded by “destiny, circumstance, and nature”.  Similar ideas seem to have been on the mind of Śvetāśvatara, who rejected the views of “time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, states of matter, wombs, and the Person” (Śvetāśvatara 1.2).
an3.61:2.2: For other refutations of this view, see [sn36.21:2.1]().
an3.61:3.3: For this refutation to be cogent, the present tense “everything an individual person experiences” must be understood as stating a general truth, rather than applying specifically to this life. If only this life was meant, then it could still be the case that present actions would affect future lives. The claim, therefore, must be, “everything an individual person experiences or will experience”. The same applies to the other tenets as well. For example, the tenet of God’s creation implies, not an initial act of creation that set the world in motion, but that the universe is sustained by the ongoing manifestation of God’s will.
an3.61:5.3: This argument speaks to the tension in theistic religions between the belief that God created everything and that individual choice matters. Religions wrestle with this in their own way, but the Buddha is arguing that if they were consistent and genuinely believed that God created everything, there would be no moral action.
